rv.q: Bloom is so good in her default mode, with a glint in her eye and dozens of curse words in her mouth, that she wins you over to her helter-skelter view of the world.
The new show toes, often dexterously, the line between confidence and vulnerability, earnest emotion and winking self-dramatization...
I can think of few more delightful, hilariously tuneful ways.
With signature panache and zero regard for propriety, Bloom uses this mawkish fantasy to tie her shambolic musings into one neat, colorful, hilarious bow.
She’s holding space for us to work through it with humor and heart.
Death, Let Me Do My Show is part stand-up comedy, part musical theatre extravaganza, and part confessional, and its effect is as disjointed as these elements.

I contend that the unapologetically aggressive Bloom – an obviously intelligent and extremely proficient presence in glittering pants suit and gold high heels – has the wherewithal to put together 85 intermissionless minutes that deal more movingly with death while remaining just as risible.
Death, Let Me Do My Show is an absolutely first-rate entertainment.
Bloom’s grief, while certainly real, sometimes feels secondhand — and her reliance on meta devices never quite give her material either heft or over-the-top hilarity.

cn.t: Bloom's raw, personal meditation on mortality earns laughs but divides critics—some find her no-filter approach brilliantly funny and moving, while others feel the show struggles to fully cohere around its pandemic-era traumas.
